Name: Leah
Transcript: Thanks for doing this. There are no right or wrong answers, it's your experience I'm interested in, and we can stop whenever you like. So, to start. Can you tell me how you came to be working from home, and what it's like for you now?

Name: Ros
Transcript: Well, I work for the council. Revenues and benefits, so council tax, housing benefit, that sort of thing. I've been there twenty-two years. And before the pandemic, working from home, you'd have had to have a very good reason, and even then your manager would look at you like you'd asked for a kidney. And then overnight we were all doing it. And it turned out the sky didn't fall in. So now it's hybrid. Two days in the office, Tuesday and Wednesday, three at home. And I love it. I'll be honest with you, I love it. I'd fight anyone who tried to take it off me.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What is it you love about it?

Name: Ros
Transcript: The time, mainly. I used to leave the house at quarter past seven to get the bus, and I'd get in at six, and that was the day gone. Now on a home day I'm up at the same time, but I take my tea out into the garden and I just stand there. Ten minutes. Looking at the beans. I'd never seen my own garden in the morning, in twenty years. Isn't that awful? It was there all along and I was on the number forty-two.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What's it like, standing there in the morning?

Name: Ros
Transcript: Peaceful. That's the only word. Nobody wants anything off me for ten minutes. And I don't know, I've got more patience on the phone now, I think, because I've had my ten minutes. Before, by the time I got to my desk I'd already had the bus and the rain and some lad's music in my ear, and I was frazzled before I'd started. Now I start the day as myself. And I'm saving a fortune on the bus, as well, and on sandwiches. That's not nothing, these days.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Can you take me through a normal working day, from when you get up?

Name: Ros
Transcript: A home day? Up at half six, tea in the garden like I said. Then I get Ollie up, he's seventeen, so that's a job in itself. He's doing his A levels. Then I'll log on at about eight, I like to start early and finish early. I'm at the kitchen table, I've got a proper chair the council gave us, a proper screen. And then it's cases, mostly. People ringing up who can't pay, or the system's charged them twice, and I sort it out. I'm good at it. At twelve I'll stop for lunch, and I'll be honest, I'll put a wash on, or nip to the Co-op. And I feel guilty about that. I do. Even though I've worked through my break, I feel like I've been caught out. And then I finish at four, half four.

Name: Leah
Transcript: You said you feel caught out.

Name: Ros
Transcript: Yes. It's daft. It's twenty years of being in an office where if you weren't at your desk, someone would say, where's Ros? So I'll be hanging the washing out and I'll have the work phone in my apron pocket, like a teenager. In case it rings and I'm not there. And it never rings. But I can't leave it on the side.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Where in your home do you work? What's that space like for you?

Name: Ros
Transcript: The kitchen table, like I said. Which I don't mind, it's a nice kitchen, it looks out on the garden. But the thing is, the work phone sits on the worktop next to the bread bin. And it goes off. At seven at night, it'll buzz, because someone in the team's put something in the group chat. And I'll look at it. I don't have to. Nobody expects me to. But it's there next to the bread bin, buzzing away. So I've started putting it in the drawer. The cutlery drawer. And then it buzzes in the drawer and the spoons rattle. Ollie thinks it's hysterical.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What happens at the start and the end of your working day?

Name: Ros
Transcript: Started is when I put my lanyard on. I know. I don't need it at home. But I put it on. It's like, that's Ros from revenues now, not Mum. And finished is when I take it off and hang it on the hook by the back door. That's my clocking off. I didn't plan it, it just happened, and now I can't not do it. If I forget to take it off, I'm still sort of at work in my head while I'm doing the tea.

Name: Leah
Transcript: How has working from home changed things with the people you live with, or the people around you?

Name: Ros
Transcript: Oh, everything. My mum, mainly. She's eighty-three, she lives about ten minutes away, on her own. And because I'm at home three days a week, I'm the one who takes her to her appointments now. Before, my brother did some of it, because he's self-employed. Now it's, well, Ros is at home. As if home means free. So I'll be on my lunch, driving her to the eye clinic, and then I'm back at the table at one with my coat still on. And I don't mind, I want to do it, she's my mum. But nobody asked me. It just landed. It landed because I was the one at home.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What was it like, when it landed?

Name: Ros
Transcript: Honestly? I was cross for about a week. And then I just got on with it, because what else are you going to do. My brother's lovely, but he's got a business, hasn't he. And I've only got a job. That's how it gets put, not in those words, but that's how it gets put. And the neighbours. Mrs Patel next door, I take her parcels in now. Everyone on the road knows I'm in on a Monday, Thursday and Friday. I'm like the depot.

Name: Leah
Transcript: The depot.

Name: Ros
Transcript: Well, that's what it feels like. Last Thursday I had six parcels in my hall, and only one of them was mine. And Ollie, he's the same. Because I'm in, he thinks I'm available. Mum, can you run me to college, Mum, can you pick me up from Jake's. On a work day. And I'll say I'm working, and he'll say, but you're at home. They all say it. You're at home. Like it's one word. Like being at home and being free are the same thing.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Can you tell me about a day working from home that has stayed with you?

Name: Ros
Transcript: There was one, it still makes me go hot. I was on a call with a woman who was being evicted, very upset, and I was trying to sort out a backdated claim for her. And Ollie came in, in his boxer shorts, and opened the fridge and said, Mum, have we got any of them yoghurts. Very loudly. And she heard. And she went quiet and then she said, you've got a family, then. And I don't know why but I felt like I'd been rude to her. Like I'd let her into my kitchen without asking her. Or let her see something she shouldn't. I put a sign on the door after that. In Sharpie. On a call, do not come in. He ignores it.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What do you miss about working somewhere else? And what would you miss if you had to go back?

Name: Ros
Transcript: I still go in two days, so I don't miss it as such. I like my office days, actually. I put my face on, I have a natter, we go to the café on a Wednesday. But I'll tell you what, I don't miss being on show all day. In the office you're always being looked at. Am I busy enough. Am I laughing at the right jokes. At home nobody's looking, and I'm a lot more myself. I get more done, as well. And if I had to go back full time? The garden in the morning. I'd miss the garden. And being there for Mum, even if it's a lot. I'd rather it was me, really. I'd rather it was me than a taxi.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Is there anything about working from home that we haven't touched on, that matters to you?

Name: Ros
Transcript: Only that people think it's for the young ones. The laptop in the coffee shop. And it's not. It's women like me, with a mum and a teenager and a bad knee, who'd have packed in work years ago if it wasn't for this. It's kept me working. I don't think the people who want us all back in realise that. And you don't moan about it, do you. Not when there's people stood at bus stops at six in the morning. You keep your head down and you count your blessings.
